We also have

questions.worked_solution:
For any linear differential operator $L,$ we have the linearity condition

$$
L(a{y}_{1}+b{y}_{2})=aL({y}_{1})+bL({y}_{2})
$$

for functions ${y}_{1}(x),{y}_{2}(x),$ and where $a$ and $b$ are constants. 

For the given differential operator, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}D(a{y}_{1}+b{y}_{2}) & =\frac{{\text{d}}^{2}}{\text{d}{x}^{2}}(a{y}_{1}+b{y}_{2})+{(\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(a{y}_{1}+b{y}_{2}))}^{2} \\  & =a\frac{{\text{d}}^{2}{y}_{1}}{\text{d}{x}^{2}}+b\frac{{\text{d}}^{2}{y}_{2}}{\text{d}{x}^{2}}+{(a\frac{\text{d}{y}_{1}}{\text{d}x}+b\frac{\text{d}{y}_{2}}{\text{d}x})}^{2} \\  & =a\frac{{\text{d}}^{2}{y}_{1}}{\text{d}{x}^{2}}+b\frac{{\text{d}}^{2}{y}_{2}}{\text{d}{x}^{2}}+{a}^{2}{(\frac{\text{d}{y}_{1}}{\text{d}x})}^{2}+2ab\frac{\text{d}{y}_{1}}{\text{d}x}\frac{\text{d}{y}_{2}}{\text{d}x}+{b}^{2}{(\frac{\text{d}{y}_{2}}{\text{d}x})}^{2} \\  & =a\frac{{\text{d}}^{2}{y}_{1}}{\text{d}{x}^{2}}+b\frac{{\text{d}}^{2}{y}_{2}}{\text{d}{x}^{2}}+{a}^{2}{(\frac{\text{d}{y}_{1}}{\text{d}x})}^{2}+{b}^{2}{(\frac{\text{d}{y}_{2}}{\text{d}x})}^{2} \\  & +2ab\cdot (\frac{\text{d}{y}_{1}}{\text{d}x}\cdot \frac{\text{d}{y}_{2}}{\text{d}x}).\end{aligned}
$$

This is *not* the same as the right-hand side, because

$$
\begin{aligned}aD({y}_{1})+bD({y}_{2}) & =a[\frac{{\text{d}}^{2}{y}_{1}}{\text{d}{x}^{2}}+{(\frac{\text{d}{y}_{1}}{\text{d}x})}^{2}]+b[\frac{{\text{d}}^{2}{y}_{2}}{\text{d}{x}^{2}}+{(\frac{\text{d}{y}_{2}}{\text{d}x})}^{2}] \\  & =a\frac{{\text{d}}^{2}{y}_{1}}{\text{d}{x}^{2}}+b\frac{{\text{d}}^{2}{y}_{2}}{\text{d}{x}^{2}}+a{(\frac{\text{d}{y}_{1}}{\text{d}x})}^{2}+b{(\frac{\text{d}{y}_{2}}{\text{d}x})}^{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, since $D(a{y}_{1}+b{y}_{2})\ne aD({y}_{1})+bD({y}_{2}),$ the operator $D$ is $\text{nonlinear}.$

questions.problem:
Which of the following are linear differential operators?

- ${D}_{1}(y)=x\frac{{\text{d}}^{2}y}{\text{d}{x}^{2}}-2xy$
- ${D}_{2}(y)={x}^{3}\frac{{\text{d}}^{2}y}{\text{d}{x}^{2}}$
- ${D}_{3}(y)=y\frac{{\text{d}}^{2}y}{\text{d}{x}^{2}}+xy$
questions.worked_solution:
For any linear differential operator,

$$
D(a{y}_{1}+b{y}_{2})=aD({y}_{1})+bD({y}_{2})
$$

where $a$ and $b$ are constants. 

Let's check each case in turn.

- The first operator is indeed linear. To see this, we check the above linearity condition:

$$
\begin{aligned}{D}_{1}(a{y}_{1}+b{y}_{2}) & =x\frac{{\text{d}}^{2}}{\text{d}{x}^{2}}(a{y}_{1}+b{y}_{2})-2x(a{y}_{1}+b{y}_{2}) \\  & =ax\frac{{\text{d}}^{2}{y}_{1}}{\text{d}{x}^{2}}+bx\frac{{\text{d}}^{2}{y}_{2}}{\text{d}{x}^{2}}-2ax{y}_{1}-2bx{y}_{2} \\  & =a[x\frac{{\text{d}}^{2}{y}_{1}}{\text{d}{x}^{2}}-2x{y}_{1}]+b[x\frac{{\text{d}}^{2}{y}_{2}}{\text{d}{x}^{2}}-2x{y}_{2}] \\  & =a{D}_{1}({y}_{1})+b{D}_{1}({y}_{2})\,✓\end{aligned}
$$

- The second operator is also linear. To see this, we check the above linearity condition:

$$
\begin{aligned}{D}_{2}(a{y}_{1}+b{y}_{2}) & ={x}^{3}\frac{{\text{d}}^{2}}{\text{d}{x}^{2}}(a{y}_{1}+b{y}_{2}) \\  & =a{x}^{3}\frac{{\text{d}}^{2}{y}_{1}}{\text{d}{x}^{2}}+b{x}^{3}\frac{{\text{d}}^{2}{y}_{2}}{\text{d}{x}^{2}} \\  & =a[{x}^{3}\frac{{\text{d}}^{2}{y}_{1}}{\text{d}{x}^{2}}]+b[{x}^{3}\frac{{\text{d}}^{2}{y}_{2}}{\text{d}{x}^{2}}] \\  & =a{D}_{2}({y}_{1})+b{D}_{2}({y}_{2})\,✓\end{aligned}
$$

- The third operator is **not** linear.
To see why, we first evaluate the left-hand side of the linearity condition:

$$
\begin{aligned}{D}_{3}(a{y}_{1}+b{y}_{2}) & =(a{y}_{1}+b{y}_{2})\frac{{\text{d}}^{2}}{\text{d}{x}^{2}}(a{y}_{1}+b{y}_{2})+x(a{y}_{1}+b{y}_{2}) \\  & =(a{y}_{1}+b{y}_{2})(a\frac{{\text{d}}^{2}{y}_{1}}{\text{d}{x}^{2}}+b\frac{{\text{d}}^{2}{y}_{2}}{\text{d}{x}^{2}})+ax{y}_{1}+bx{y}_{2} \\  & ={a}^{2}{y}_{1}\frac{{\text{d}}^{2}{y}_{1}}{\text{d}{x}^{2}}+{b}^{2}{y}_{2}\frac{{\text{d}}^{2}{y}_{2}}{\text{d}{x}^{2}}+ab({y}_{1}\frac{{\text{d}}^{2}{y}_{2}}{\text{d}{x}^{2}}+{y}_{2}\frac{{\text{d}}^{2}{y}_{1}}{\text{d}{x}^{2}})+ax{y}_{1}+bx{y}_{2}\end{aligned}
$$

This is not the same as the right-hand side, because

$$
\begin{aligned}a{D}_{3}({y}_{1})+b{D}_{3}({y}_{2}) & =a[{y}_{1}\frac{{\text{d}}^{2}{y}_{1}}{\text{d}{x}^{2}}+x{y}_{1}]+b[{y}_{2}\frac{{\text{d}}^{2}{y}_{2}}{\text{d}{x}^{2}}+x{y}_{2}] \\  & =a{y}_{1}\frac{{\text{d}}^{2}{y}_{1}}{\text{d}{x}^{2}}+b{y}_{2}\frac{{\text{d}}^{2}{y}_{2}}{\text{d}{x}^{2}}+ax{y}_{1}+bx{y}_{2}.\,\times \end{aligned}
$$

questions.problem:
Which of the following are linear differential operators?

- ${D}_{1}(y)={x}^{3}\frac{{\text{d}}^{2}y}{\text{d}{x}^{2}}+{x}^{2}y$
- ${D}_{2}(y)=y\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}+2y$
- ${D}_{3}(y)=\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}+xy$
questions.worked_solution:
For any linear differential operator,

$$
D(a{y}_{1}+b{y}_{2})=aD({y}_{1})+bD({y}_{2})
$$

where $a$ and $b$ are constants. 

Let's check each case in turn.

- The first operator is indeed linear. To see this, we check the above linearity condition:

$$
\begin{aligned}{D}_{1}(a{y}_{1}+b{y}_{2}) & ={x}^{3}\frac{{\text{d}}^{2}}{\text{d}{x}^{2}}(a{y}_{1}+b{y}_{2})+{x}^{2}(a{y}_{1}+b{y}_{2}) \\  & =a{x}^{3}\frac{{\text{d}}^{2}{y}_{1}}{\text{d}{x}^{2}}+b{x}^{3}\frac{{\text{d}}^{2}{y}_{2}}{\text{d}{x}^{2}}+a{x}^{2}{y}_{1}+a{x}^{2}{y}_{2} \\  & =a[{x}^{3}\frac{{\text{d}}^{2}{y}_{1}}{\text{d}{x}^{2}}+{x}^{2}{y}_{1}]+b[{x}^{3}\frac{{\text{d}}^{2}{y}_{2}}{\text{d}{x}^{2}}+{x}^{2}{y}_{2}] \\  & =a{D}_{1}({y}_{1})+b{D}_{1}({y}_{2})\,✓\end{aligned}
$$

- The second operator is **not** linear.
To see why, we first evaluate the left-hand side of the linearity condition:

$$
\begin{aligned}{D}_{2}(a{y}_{1}+b{y}_{2}) & =(a{y}_{1}+b{y}_{2})\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(a{y}_{1}+b{y}_{2})+2(a{y}_{1}+b{y}_{2}) \\  & =(a{y}_{1}+b{y}_{2})(a\frac{\text{d}{y}_{1}}{\text{d}x}+b\frac{\text{d}{y}_{2}}{\text{d}x})+2a{y}_{1}+2b{y}_{2} \\  & ={a}^{2}{y}_{1}\frac{\text{d}{y}_{1}}{\text{d}x}+{b}^{2}{y}_{2}\frac{\text{d}{y}_{2}}{\text{d}x}+ab({y}_{1}\frac{\text{d}{y}_{2}}{\text{d}x}+{y}_{2}\frac{\text{d}{y}_{1}}{\text{d}x})+2a{y}_{1}+2b{y}_{2}\end{aligned}
$$

This is not the same as the right-hand side, because

$$
\begin{aligned}a{D}_{2}({y}_{1})+b{D}_{2}({y}_{2}) & =a[{y}_{1}\frac{\text{d}{y}_{1}}{\text{d}x}+2{y}_{1}]+b[{y}_{2}\frac{\text{d}{y}_{2}}{\text{d}x}+2{y}_{2}] \\  & =a{y}_{1}\frac{\text{d}{y}_{1}}{\text{d}x}+b{y}_{2}\frac{\text{d}{y}_{2}}{\text{d}x}+2a{y}_{1}+2b{y}_{2}.\,\times \end{aligned}
$$

- The third operator is also linear. To see this, we check the above linearity condition:

$$
\begin{aligned}{D}_{3}(a{y}_{1}+b{y}_{2}) & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(a{y}_{1}+b{y}_{2})+x(a{y}_{1}+b{y}_{2}) \\  & =a\frac{\text{d}{y}_{1}}{\text{d}x}+b\frac{\text{d}{y}_{2}}{\text{d}x}+ax{y}_{1}+bx{y}_{2} \\  & =a[\frac{\text{d}{y}_{1}}{\text{d}x}+x{y}_{1}]+b[\frac{\text{d}{y}_{2}}{\text{d}x}+x{y}_{2}] \\  & =a{D}_{3}({y}_{1})+b{D}_{3}({y}_{2})\,✓\end{aligned}
$$

for functions ${y}_{1}(x),{y}_{2}(x),$ and where $a$ and $b$ are constants.

$$
\begin{aligned}aD({y}_{1})+bD({y}_{2}) & =a[{(\frac{\text{d}{y}_{1}}{\text{d}x})}^{2}+{y}_{1}]+b[{(\frac{\text{d}{y}_{2}}{\text{d}x})}^{2}+{y}_{2}] \\  & =a{(\frac{\text{d}{y}_{1}}{\text{d}x})}^{2}+b{(\frac{\text{d}{y}_{2}}{\text{d}x})}^{2}+a{y}_{1}+b{y}_{2}.\end{aligned}

questions.problem:
Which of the following are linear differential operators?

- ${D}_{1}(y)=xy\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}+\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}$
- ${D}_{2}(y)=\operatorname{cos}⁡(x)\frac{{\text{d}}^{2}y}{\text{d}{x}^{2}}+{x}^{2}\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}+{e}^{x}y$
- ${D}_{3}(y)=\frac{{\text{d}}^{3}y}{\text{d}{x}^{3}}+\operatorname{tan}⁡(y)\,y$
questions.worked_solution:
An $n$th-order differential operator $L$ is linear if it is of the following form:

$$
L(y)={f}_{n}(x)\frac{{\text{d}}^{n}y}{\text{d}{x}^{n}}+{f}_{n-1}(x)\frac{{\text{d}}^{n-1}y}{\text{d}{x}^{n-1}}+⋯+{f}_{1}(x)\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}+{f}_{0}(x)y
$$

where each ${f}_{i}$ is a function of $x$ only. 

With that in mind, let's check each operator.

- Operator ${D}_{1}$ is *not* linear. The coefficient of the first term is $xy,$ which depends on $y$ and therefore fails linearity.

- Operator ${D}_{2}$ is linear. It is a second-order linear differential operator of the form

$$
{D}_{2}(y)={f}_{2}(x)\frac{{\text{d}}^{2}y}{\text{d}{x}^{2}}+{f}_{1}(x)\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}+{f}_{0}(x)y
$$

with ${f}_{2}(x)=\operatorname{cos}⁡(x),{f}_{1}(x)={x}^{2},$ and ${f}_{0}(x)={e}^{x}.$

- Operator ${D}_{3}$ is *not* linear. The coefficient of the last term is $\operatorname{tan}⁡(y),$ which depends on $y$ and therefore fails linearity.

Therefore, the correct answer is "II only."

questions.problem:
Which of the following are linear differential operators?

- ${D}_{1}(y)=(x-1)\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}+2xy$
- ${D}_{2}(y)=y\frac{{\text{d}}^{2}y}{\text{d}{x}^{2}}+\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}$
- ${D}_{3}(y)=4\frac{{\text{d}}^{3}y}{\text{d}{x}^{3}}-{x}^{2}\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}+xy$
questions.worked_solution:
An $n$th-order differential operator $L$ is linear if it is of the following form:

$$
L(y)={f}_{n}(x)\frac{{\text{d}}^{n}y}{\text{d}{x}^{n}}+{f}_{n-1}(x)\frac{{\text{d}}^{n-1}y}{\text{d}{x}^{n-1}}+⋯+{f}_{1}(x)\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}+{f}_{0}(x)y
$$

where each ${f}_{i}$ is a function of $x$ only. 

With that in mind, let's check each operator.

- Operator ${D}_{1}$ is linear. It is a first-order linear differential operator of the form

$$
{D}_{1}(y)={f}_{1}(x)\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}+{f}_{0}(x)y
$$

with ${f}_{1}(x)=x-1$ and ${f}_{0}(x)=2x.$

- Operator ${D}_{2}$ is *not* linear. The coefficient of the first term is $y,$ which depends on $y$ and therefore fails linearity.

- Operator ${D}_{3}$ is linear. It is a third-order linear differential operator of the form

$$
{D}_{3}(y)={f}_{3}(x)\frac{{\text{d}}^{3}y}{\text{d}{x}^{3}}+{f}_{2}(x)\frac{{\text{d}}^{2}y}{\text{d}{x}^{2}}+{f}_{1}(x)\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}+{f}_{0}(x)y
$$

with ${f}_{3}(x)=4,{f}_{2}(x)=0,{f}_{1}(x)=-{x}^{2},$ and ${f}_{0}(x)=x.$

Therefore, the correct answer is "I and III only."

questions.knowledge_point: Identifying Linear Differential Operators Using the General Form
questions.problem:
Which of the following are linear differential operators?

- ${D}_{1}(y)=\frac{1}{x+1}\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}+\operatorname{sin}⁡(x)\,y$
- ${D}_{2}(y)=\sqrt{x}\frac{{\text{d}}^{2}y}{\text{d}{x}^{2}}-\operatorname{ln}⁡(x)\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}-2y$
- ${D}_{3}(y)=2\frac{{\text{d}}^{3}y}{\text{d}{x}^{3}}+{e}^{x}\frac{{\text{d}}^{2}y}{\text{d}{x}^{2}}-\frac{1}{1+{x}^{2}}\,y$
questions.worked_solution:
An $n$th-order differential operator $L$ is linear if it is of the following form:

$$
L(y)={f}_{n}(x)\frac{{\text{d}}^{n}y}{\text{d}{x}^{n}}+{f}_{n-1}(x)\frac{{\text{d}}^{n-1}y}{\text{d}{x}^{n-1}}+⋯+{f}_{1}(x)\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}+{f}_{0}(x)y
$$

where each ${f}_{i}$ is a function of $x$ only. 

With that in mind, let's check each operator.

- Operator ${D}_{1}$ is linear. It is a first-order linear differential operator of the form

$$
{D}_{1}(y)={f}_{1}(x)\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}+{f}_{0}(x)y
$$

with ${f}_{1}(x)=\frac{1}{x+1}$ and ${f}_{0}(x)=\operatorname{sin}⁡(x).$

- Operator ${D}_{2}$ is linear. It is a second-order linear differential operator of the form

$$
{D}_{2}(y)={f}_{2}(x)\frac{{\text{d}}^{2}y}{\text{d}{x}^{2}}+{f}_{1}(x)\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}+{f}_{0}(x)y
$$

with ${f}_{2}(x)=\sqrt{x},{f}_{1}(x)=-\operatorname{ln}⁡(x),$ and ${f}_{0}(x)=-2.$

- Operator ${D}_{3}$ is linear. It is a third-order linear differential operator of the form

$$
{D}_{3}(y)={f}_{3}(x)\frac{{\text{d}}^{3}y}{\text{d}{x}^{3}}+{f}_{2}(x)\frac{{\text{d}}^{2}y}{\text{d}{x}^{2}}+{f}_{1}(x)\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}+{f}_{0}(x)y
$$

with ${f}_{3}(x)=2,{f}_{2}(x)={e}^{x},{f}_{1}(x)=0,$ and ${f}_{0}(x)=-\frac{1}{1+{x}^{2}}.$

Therefore, the correct answer is "I, II, and III."

questions.problem: Suppose that $L$ is a linear differential operator such that $L({y}_{1})=2{cos}^{2}⁡x$ and $L({y}_{2})={sin}^{2}⁡x+4$ for some functions ${y}_{1}(x)$ and ${y}_{2}(x).$ What is $L({y}_{1}+2{y}_{2})?$
questions.worked_solution:
For any linear differential operator,

$$
L(a{y}_{1}(x)+b{y}_{2}(x))=aL({y}_{1}(x))+bL({y}_{2}(x))
$$

where $a$ and $b$ are constants. 

In our case, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}L({y}_{1}+2{y}_{2}) & =L({y}_{1})+2L({y}_{2}) \\  & =2{cos}^{2}⁡x+2\cdot ({sin}^{2}⁡x+4) \\  & =2{cos}^{2}⁡x+2{sin}^{2}⁡x+8 \\  & =2({cos}^{2}⁡x+{sin}^{2}⁡x)+8 \\  & =2+8 \\  & =10.\end{aligned}
$$

questions.problem: Suppose that $L$ is a linear differential operator such that $L({y}_{1})={x}^{2}-3x$ and $L({y}_{2})=x(x+1)$ for some functions ${y}_{1}(x)$ and ${y}_{2}(x).$ What is $L({y}_{1}+3{y}_{2})?$
questions.worked_solution:
For any linear differential operator,

$$
L(a{y}_{1}(x)+b{y}_{2}(x))=aL({y}_{1}(x))+bL({y}_{2}(x))
$$

where $a$ and $b$ are constants. 

In our case, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}L({y}_{1}+3{y}_{2}) & =L({y}_{1})+3L({y}_{2}) \\  & ={x}^{2}-3x+3\cdot x(x+1) \\  & ={x}^{2}-3x+3{x}^{2}+3x \\  & =({x}^{2}+3{x}^{2})+(3x-3x) \\  & =4{x}^{2}+0 \\  & =4{x}^{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

where $a$ and $b$ are constants.

where $a$ and $b$ are constants.

canonical_examples.problem:
Show that the differential operator

$$
D(y) = y\dfrac{\textrm d^2 y}{\textrm d x^2} + \dfrac{\textrm d y}{\textrm d x}
$$

is nonlinear.
canonical_examples.worked_solution:
For any linear differential operator $L,$ we have the linearity condition

$$
L(ay_1 + by_2) = aL(y_1) + bL(y_2)
$$

for functions $y_1(x), y_2(x),$ and where $a$ and $b$ are constants. 

For the given differential operator, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}D(a{y}_{1}+b{y}_{2}) & =(a{y}_{1}+b{y}_{2})\frac{{\text{d}}^{2}}{\text{d}{x}^{2}}(a{y}_{1}+b{y}_{2})+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(a{y}_{1}+b{y}_{2}) \\  & =(a{y}_{1}+b{y}_{2})(a\frac{{\text{d}}^{2}{y}_{1}}{\text{d}{x}^{2}}+b\frac{{\text{d}}^{2}{y}_{2}}{\text{d}{x}^{2}})+a\frac{\text{d}{y}_{1}}{\text{d}x}+b\frac{\text{d}{y}_{2}}{\text{d}x} \\  & =+{a}^{2}{y}_{1}\frac{{\text{d}}^{2}{y}_{1}}{\text{d}{x}^{2}}+ab{y}_{1}\frac{{\text{d}}^{2}{y}_{2}}{\text{d}{x}^{2}}+ab{y}_{2}\frac{{\text{d}}^{2}{y}_{1}}{\text{d}{x}^{2}}+{b}^{2}{y}_{2}\frac{{\text{d}}^{2}{y}_{2}}{\text{d}{x}^{2}} \\  & +a\frac{\text{d}{y}_{1}}{\text{d}x}+b\frac{\text{d}{y}_{2}}{\text{d}x} \\  & ={a}^{2}{y}_{1}\frac{{\text{d}}^{2}{y}_{1}}{\text{d}{x}^{2}}+{b}^{2}{y}_{2}\frac{{\text{d}}^{2}{y}_{2}}{\text{d}{x}^{2}}+a\frac{\text{d}{y}_{1}}{\text{d}x}+b\frac{\text{d}{y}_{2}}{\text{d}x} \\  & +ab({y}_{1}\frac{{\text{d}}^{2}{y}_{2}}{\text{d}{x}^{2}}+{y}_{2}\frac{{\text{d}}^{2}{y}_{1}}{\text{d}{x}^{2}}).\end{aligned}
$$

This is *not* the same as the right-hand side, because

$$
\begin{aligned}aD({y}_{1})+bD({y}_{2}) & =a[{y}_{1}\frac{{\text{d}}^{2}{y}_{1}}{\text{d}{x}^{2}}+\frac{\text{d}{y}_{1}}{\text{d}x}]+b[{y}_{2}\frac{{\text{d}}^{2}{y}_{2}}{\text{d}{x}^{2}}+\frac{\text{d}{y}_{2}}{\text{d}x}] \\  & =a{y}_{1}\frac{{\text{d}}^{2}{y}_{1}}{\text{d}{x}^{2}}+b{y}_{2}\frac{{\text{d}}^{2}{y}_{2}}{\text{d}{x}^{2}}+a\frac{\text{d}{y}_{1}}{\text{d}x}+b\frac{\text{d}{y}_{2}}{\text{d}x}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, since $D(ay_1+by_2)  \neq aD(y_1) + bD(y_2),$ the operator $D$ is nonlinear.

canonical_examples.knowledge_point: Identifying Linear Differential Operators Using the General Form
canonical_examples.problem:
Which of the following are linear differential operators?

- $D_1(y)=\dfrac{\textrm dy}{\textrm d x}+x\cos(y)\,y$

- $D_2(y)=\dfrac{1}{1+x^2}\dfrac{\textrm d^{2}y}{\textrm d x^{2}}-\sin(x)\dfrac{\textrm dy}{\textrm d x}+3y$

- $D_3(y)=\dfrac{\textrm d^{3}y}{\textrm d x^{3}}+e^{x}\dfrac{\textrm d^{2}y}{\textrm d x^{2}}-\ln(x)\,y$
canonical_examples.worked_solution:
An $n$th-order differential operator $L$ is linear if it is of the following form:

$$
L(y) = f_{n}(x)\dfrac{\textrm d^{n}y}{\textrm d x^{n}} + f_{n-1}(x)\dfrac{\textrm d^{n-1}y}{\textrm d x^{n-1}} + \cdots + f_{1}(x)\dfrac{\textrm dy}{\textrm d x} + f_0(x)y
$$

where each $f_i$ is a function of $x$ only. 

With that in mind, let's check each operator.

- Operator $D_1$ is *not* linear. The coefficient of the second term is $x\cos(y),$ which depends on $y$ and therefore fails linearity.

- Operator $D_2$ is linear. It is a second-order linear differential operator of the form

$$
D_2(y) = f_{2}(x)\dfrac{\textrm d^{2}y}{\textrm d x^{2}} + f_{1}(x)\dfrac{\textrm dy}{\textrm d x} + f_0(x)y
$$

with $f_2(x) = \dfrac{1}{1+x^2}, f_1(x) = -\sin(x),$ and $f_0(x) = 3.$

- Operator $D_3$ is linear. It is a third-order linear differential operator of the form

$$
D_3(y) = f_{3}(x)\dfrac{\textrm d^{3}y}{\textrm d x^{3}} + f_{2}(x)\dfrac{\textrm d^{2}y}{\textrm d x^{2}} + f_{1}(x)\dfrac{\textrm dy}{\textrm d x} + f_0(x)y
$$

with $f_3(x) = 1, f_2(x) = e^{x}, f_1(x) = 0,$ and $f_0(x) = -\ln(x).$

Therefore, the correct answer is "II and III only."

canonical_examples.problem:
Suppose that $L$ is a linear differential operator such that $L(y_1) = \tan^2{x}$ and $L(y_2) =2 \sec^2{x}$ for some functions $y_1(x)$ and $y_2(x).$ What is $L(2y_1 -y_2)?$

*Hint: Use $\sec^2\theta = 1+\tan^2\theta.$*
canonical_examples.worked_solution:
For any linear differential operator $L,$ we have

$$
L(ay_1(x) + by_2(x)) = aL(y_1(x)) + bL(y_2(x))
$$

where $a$ and $b$ are constants. 

In our case, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}L(2{y}_{1}-{y}_{2}) & =2L({y}_{1})-L({y}_{2}) \\  & =2{tan}^{2}⁡x-2{sec}^{2}⁡x.\end{aligned}
$$

Using the trigonometric identity $1+\tan^2 x = \sec^2 x,$ we can simplify this even further, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}L(2{y}_{1}-{y}_{2}) & =2{tan}^{2}⁡x-2(1+{tan}^{2}⁡x) \\  & =-2.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, 

$$
L(2y_1 -y_2)=-2.
$$
